title: The Bus Stop Designed Around Waiting
passage:
A city planned to replace old bus shelters along a busy suburban road. The original proposal focused on appearance. The new shelters would use glass walls, narrow metal benches, and a common color scheme. Before ordering dozens of identical units, the transport department built one prototype and asked passengers to use it for a month.

The prototype looked modern, but complaints arrived quickly. On sunny afternoons, the glass trapped heat. The narrow bench was difficult for some older passengers to use because it had no back support. Parents with strollers could enter the shelter, but if two strollers were present there was little room for anyone to pass. During heavy rain, wind pushed water through the open side. The shelter met basic design standards, yet daily experience revealed weaknesses.

Engineers initially tried to solve each complaint by adding something: a sun film on the glass, a wider bench, another side panel. An accessibility adviser suggested stepping back. Rather than treating the shelter as a small building, the team should study the act of waiting. Who waited, for how long, at what times, and what did they need to see or do while waiting?

Observers spent several days at six bus stops. They found that needs differed sharply. Near the hospital, many passengers were older and waits were often ten to fifteen minutes. Near the secondary school, crowds were large but waits were shorter. At the shopping center, people carried bags and needed more standing space. At a rural-edge stop, passengers wanted protection from wind more than shade.

The city abandoned the idea of one identical shelter. It created three modules using the same basic parts. The hospital version had more seating with backs and armrests. The school version had less seating but more open standing space and a wider entrance. The windy locations received deeper side panels, while hotter sites used roofs that projected farther outward and less glass on the west side. All versions kept clear sight lines so passengers could see approaching buses.

Digital information screens were also reconsidered. The original plan placed a large display in the center. Users with low vision appreciated bright text, but some standing passengers blocked it. The screen was moved higher, and a smaller audio button announced the next buses. The department tested the volume carefully so that it could be heard nearby without disturbing neighboring homes.

After the shelters were installed, the city continued to collect comments. One location still flooded during storms because water flowed from the road toward the curb. That problem could not be solved by changing the shelter; drainage work was required. The project reminded officials that not every discomfort experienced at a bus stop is caused by the bus-stop structure itself.

The final shelters were less visually uniform than the original design competition had imagined, but they shared a common identity and worked better in their locations. The city learned that standardization can reduce cost, yet too much standardization assumes that every situation is equivalent. Designing around waiting rather than around the object changed the question from ‘What should a bus shelter look like?’ to ‘What support does a person need here while waiting for a bus?’ That question produced more varied answers, but also more useful ones.
translation:
市は郊外の古いバス停を更新する計画を立て、当初はガラス壁、細い金属ベンチ、統一色の近代的なデザインを考えていました。しかし大量発注前に試作品を一か月使ってもらうと、問題が次々に見つかりました。

午後はガラス内が暑くなり、背もたれのない細いベンチは高齢者に使いにくく、ベビーカーが二台入ると通路が狭くなりました。強い雨では横から水が入りました。基準を満たしていても、日常利用では不足があったのです。

最初は個別に部品を追加して直そうとしましたが、アクセシビリティ担当者は『建物を作るのではなく、待つという行為を調べよう』と提案しました。誰が、どのくらい、いつ待ち、その間に何が必要なのかを観察しました。

病院前では高齢者が多く待ち時間も長い。学校前では人数が多いが待ち時間は短い。商業施設では荷物を持つ人が多く、郊外端では日陰より防風が重要でした。

そこで同一型をやめ、共通部品から三種類の構成を作りました。病院前は背もたれと肘掛け付き座席を増やし、学校前は立ちスペースを広げ、風の強い場所は側面を深く、暑い場所は屋根を広くして西側のガラスを減らしました。どれもバスが見える視界は保ちました。

運行表示も中央の大画面だけでは人に隠れるため位置を上げ、次のバスを音声で知らせる小さなボタンも追加しました。音量は周辺住宅へ迷惑をかけないよう調整しました。

設置後も調査を続けると、ある場所では道路から水が流れ込み、これは停留所ではなく排水工事が必要だと分かりました。

完成形は当初ほど均一ではありませんが、場所ごとの使いやすさは向上しました。標準化はコストを下げますが、すべての場所が同じだと仮定しすぎると問題が起きます。『どんな停留所を作るか』ではなく『ここで待つ人に何が必要か』と問うことで、より実用的な答えが得られたのです。
